synopsis: Immature technology at commitment is the corpus’s most consistently documented cause of schedule failure; late integration, unstable requirements and supplier lead times compound the risk, and independent review cannot rescue incomplete engineering late in a project [f204, f9643, f9644, f9647, f1056]. Barrick’s experience illustrates the consequences: systems were abandoned after supplier claims failed in field use and costs escalated, while its multi-year program encountered detection failures, nuisance alarms, installation problems and operator-acceptance difficulties [f10736, f10858]. For this program’s four-month validation window, unresolved hazard analysis, performance-level allocation or pass/fail metrics in 2027 signal that requirements debate may consume the available time [f12458]. Toolchain credibility requires agreed correlation metrics by the first quarter of 2027; the overriding warning is inability, by the first half of 2027, to demonstrate an auditable chain from a real test through the model and virtual result to a residual-risk decision for one representative requirement [f10756, f12196, f12462]. Planning should expose vulnerable assumptions, assign warning signs and contingencies, and exercise integration early, especially because documented escalation of commitment can keep failing projects alive [f9558, f9674, f9646, f9447, f9681]. Important uncertainties remain: compute and defect triage are proposed bottlenecks without program-specific evidence, and the claim that test volume explains a three-to-four-year off-road development duration is unproven; requirements definition is only a suspected alternative bottleneck [f10789, f10790, f10853, f12186].
